arguments.literal: A declared refinement answers a different question, keeps its own vocabulary and declares a total mapping to the core; no refinement adds a core member.

A project adopts the profile by: naming it in its UX-related design modules; recording the realisation stack choice and justification; declaring the irreducible architectural carrier set and structural carrier diagram (DESIGN_MODULE §6, §7); declaring the State, Msg, Update, Cmd and Sub shapes for each UX surface in the design module before implementation; declaring the typed-contract bindings the surface consumes and emits to (§7); naming the effect-membrane mechanism and the Cmd algebra it interprets (§6); naming the executable Msg-replay proof surface (§8); naming any §11 accessibility refinement; noting any §9 view-shape or §6 effect-membrane exemptions explicitly. Adoption is per project and may cover only some UX surfaces, with the scope recorded in the design module.
UX §12; P2, P4b, P6

Side effects are isolated to a declared effect membrane, which refines DESIGN_MODULE §10 Effect edge for UX surfaces. The membrane interprets Cmd values produced by the reducer and translates side-effect outcomes back into Msg values delivered to the reducer. Inside the membrane, I/O, subscriptions to external sources and imperative interop with the host platform (DOM, file system, native APIs) are allowed. Outside it, in render code, in pure helpers consumed by render, and in the reducer, there is no I/O, no subscription and no imperative platform manipulation.
UX §6; P0, P5

The membrane has one job: interpret declared Cmd values; it is not where logic lives. Branching, conditional state derivation and multi-step business decisions belong in the reducer; the membrane interprets a single declared Cmd per effect. A platform-specific effect handler, whatever the framework calls it (useEffect, createEffect, onMount, subscribe, a server-action handler), is part of the membrane only when it interprets a declared Cmd. A handler that contains conditional logic deciding state transitions is a violation: the logic moves to the reducer, and the handler interprets one Cmd.
UX §6; P1, P6

Every product UX surface carries at least one executable Msg-replay proof for each product-meaningful interaction family before claiming closure under this profile. A replay proof includes: an initial State fixture; an ordered Msg log; the expected final State; the expected ordered Cmd values; the success and failure Msg values returned by interpreted Cmds; injected deterministic values for time, randomness, generated ids and external payloads. The proof fails if correctness depends on: DOM state not represented in State; mutable refs, module variables, closures, timers or effect-handler memory; network or file results that bypass typed Msg; view-local state that changes product behaviour after unmount or replay. For a pure projection-only surface the proof may be a no-effect proof: a Msg log, the final State and an empty Cmd sequence.
UX §8 Msg-replay proof; P2, P4b, P5, P6

The constitutional process model of UX work is the Elm Architecture. State: the typed state shape, held by the runtime, not by the view. Msg: the typed message algebra naming every action a user or system can emit. Update: the pure reducer (Msg, State) -> (State, Cmd); it describes side effects as Cmd values and does not perform them. View: the pure function State -> ViewTree; the same state gives the same output. Cmd and Sub: typed descriptions of side effects to schedule and of external sources to subscribe to, interpreted by the runtime at the effect membrane. The runtime owns the loop: current State -> render View -> user emits Msg -> Update produces new State and Cmds -> runtime interprets Cmds -> repeat.
UX §4; P0, P1

Each verdict answers its own question and maps as stated; nothing is coerced to satisfied. (1) compliant: do §4 to §10 hold under inspection with no §13 failure pattern present -> satisfied (this row applies the stricter of two compliance tests that disagree, §4 Realisation discretion against the §12 compliance criterion; the choice is pending Jim's ruling and is not settled by the mapping). (2) violation, including constitutionally rejected (§4): is a §13 failure pattern present -> falsified, the pattern present being the counterexample. (3) replay proof passes or fails (§8): does the proof reproduce the expected final State and Cmd sequence without a dependency §8 lists -> satisfied when it passes, falsified when it fails. (4) closure claimed without the §8 proof or the §11 obligations (§12): does every product-meaningful interaction family carry its proof and the surface its accessibility declarations, absent a recorded exemption -> falsified, the family or obligation without proof being the counterexample; inside an open UX sprint the gap is escrow and closure is not claimed. (5) blocked for want of a carrier (§3, §7): does a product-truth-changing message or action have an admitted carrier or typed contract -> the surface's evaluation is falsified (§13 pattern 13); the construction step stops as ACTIVATION §3 re_entry_requested, core out_of_frame, naming the missing carrier, its owner and the re-entry. (6) fails closed (§1 Authority): is the surface compliant where the profile is ambiguous for the case -> the stricter reading's result where that reading is fixed; out_of_frame where the ambiguity leaves a term the claim depends on undefined, naming the term and its owner; indeterminate only where the stricter reading is fixed and admissible evidence cannot decide; never satisfied by the ambiguity alone. (7) design module incomplete (§14): can each review question be answered from the design module -> invalid_basis. Collisions: blocked for want of a carrier is not ACTIVATION §3's ambiguity outcome blocked; design module incomplete is not the construction availability member incomplete.
UX §15; the one-algebra rule of ACTIVATION §3; P1, P5, P6

A scaffold, prototype, debug pane or temporary proof surface may be exempt only when the design module or ticket records all of: the exemption scope; the permitted operations; whether mutation is forbidden or explicitly bounded; a visible scaffold or debug label where user-facing; the authoritative surface that will supersede it; the retirement condition and owning ticket; the non-closure condition preventing release if the scaffold remains. An exempt scaffold cannot become the production UX by accumulation: it is retired, repriced into a governed UX surface, or kept outside product closure. An exempt scaffold is a recorded scope, not a result; evaluations outside its recorded scope proceed under the §15 table.
UX §12 Scaffold and exemption, §15; P4b, P6

The implementation stack (language, framework or runtime, state container, effect-interpreter mechanism, runtime validator, toolchain) is the project's choice, recorded in its design module with a short justification of how each choice preserves the §4 process model and the §6 effect-membrane rule; the profile does not rank stacks, it tests realisations. Constitutionally rejected, regardless of stack: a realisation that lets the view own state continuation, performs side effects in render code, mutates state outside a typed reducer, or carries multi-step view-local state machines that bypass Msg; two-way binding without Msg emission, imperative DOM manipulation in render code, and effect handlers used as controllers are violations. Compliance: §4 Process model without stack mandate says any realisation that preserves §4 to §8 is compliant; §4 Realisation discretion says a realisation is compliant when §4 to §10 hold under inspection and the §13 failure patterns are absent.
UX §4 Process model without stack mandate, §4 Realisation discretion; P1, P2, P6

A UX surface is governed by this profile by default when any of these is true: it is reachable from the product shell; it is used as proof for a ticket, requirement, design module, release or review; it can mutate product truth; it can spawn, attach, resume or dispatch work; it can change Context, selection authority, closure, continuation, evidence or provenance.
UX §12 Scaffold and exemption; P5, P6

The view does not own state continuation; state transitions flow through declared Msg actions interpreted by the reducer. A view does not decide on its own what the next state will be after a user event; does not chain several state updates locally without emitting them as separate Msg values; does not carry hidden inter-event state in refs, closures or module-level variables. A multi-step local state machine belongs in the reducer as part of State, with explicit Msg transitions between phases; the view becomes a pure projection of its phase. The Msg-replay test: can the view's behaviour be replayed by replaying its Msg log against an empty State? If not, continuation has leaked into the view.
UX §8; P0, P1, P4b, P6

frame_indexes.scope: Evaluate one UX surface under the UX profile: the Elm process model and the rejected realisations, the effect membrane and the one-Cmd handler rule, the view's non-ownership of continuation and the Msg-replay proof required before closure, adoption declarations, the scaffold law with its seven exemption records, and the total mapping of profile verdicts to the core. Selected for F-03 task G.
